evidence.claim: The Conestoga Ridge Byway carries PA 23 through Lancaster County farmland between Blue Ball and PA 10 west of Morgantown.
evidence.quote: The Conestoga Ridge Byway runs along PA 23 between US 322 in Blue Ball and PA 10 west of Morgantown, passing through farmland in Lancaster County

evidence.claim: PennDOT describes a ridge overlooking the Conestoga River and valleys, with small Amish and Mennonite farms and wooded hillsides.
evidence.quote: Following the ridge, overlooking sweeping views of the Conestoga River and valleys, one quietly travels back in time. Rolling hills with small Amish and Mennonite farmland landscape valleys bordered by forested hillsides.

evidence.claim: Designated in 2013, the byway runs through Goodville and Churchtown, where the highway serves as Main Street.
evidence.quote: along with the communities of Goodville and Churchtown. The byway was designated in 2013.

evidence.claim: where the highway serves as Main Street.
evidence.quote: Pennsylvania Route 23 is the community's Main Street

evidence.claim: This stretch belonged to the Morgantown, Churchtown, and Blue Ball Turnpike, chartered in 1814 and completed in 1819.
evidence.quote: The Morgantown, Churchtown, and Blue Ball Turnpike was chartered on February 25, 1814.

evidence.claim: Built along the Horse-Shoe Road, the turnpike connected Blue Ball with Little Conestoga in Morgantown.
evidence.quote: This turnpike, which was built along the Horse-Shoe Road and ran between the Downingtown and Harrisburg Turnpike at Blue Ball and Little Conestoga in Morgantown, was finished in 1819.

evidence.claim: PA 23 received its number in 1927 as part of a longer highway from Lancaster toward Philadelphia; its entire length was paved when designated.
evidence.quote: In 1927, PA 23 was designated to run from US 230/PA 41/PA 72 (Prince Street) in Lancaster east to City Avenue on the border of Philadelphia.

evidence.claim: its entire length was paved when designated.
evidence.quote: When first designated, the entire length of the route was paved.

evidence.claim: Start eastward at Blue Ball’s US 322 crossroads, then follow PA 23 through farmland and Goodville.
evidence.quote: The road runs through more farmland, passing through the residential community of Goodville

evidence.claim: The road crosses the Conestoga River before entering Churchtown.
evidence.quote: The route crosses the Conestoga River and runs through Churchtown.

evidence.claim: Beyond the village it curves north-northeast through rural country to PA 10, the byway’s eastern boundary west of Morgantown.
evidence.quote: The road curves north-northeast through more rural areas, passing north of Conestoga Christian School before coming to an intersection with PA 10.

evidence.claim: Blue Ball’s US 322 crossroads
evidence.quote: crossing US 322 in the community of Blue Ball.

evidence.claim: A hanging sign gave Blue Ball its name; the inn that carried it is gone.
evidence.quote: He hung a blue ball out front from a post and called it "The Sign of the Blue Ball".

evidence.claim: Early in the eighteenth century, John Wallace built at the meeting of the Native American French Creek Path and Paxtang trail, now associated with PA 23 and US 322.
evidence.quote: In the early 18th century, John Wallace built a small building in Earl Town at the intersection of two trails created by native Americans, French Creek Path (Route 23) and Paxtang (Route 322).

evidence.claim: Local usage followed his blue-ball sign, and Earl Town formally became Blue Ball in 1833.
evidence.quote: Locals soon began calling the town "Blue Ball" after the inn. In 1833, Earl Town officially changed its name to Blue Ball.

evidence.claim: The inn later took the name Blue Ball Hotel and was demolished in 1997.
evidence.quote: The inn was torn down in 1997.

evidence.claim: The two highways continue to meet in the center of town.
evidence.quote: U.S. Route 322 (Division Highway) crosses PA 23 in the center of Blue Ball;

evidence.claim: The inn later took the name Blue Ball Hotel
evidence.quote: During Prohibition, the inn changed its name to Blue Ball Hotel.

evidence.claim: PA 23 serves as Main Street in Churchtown, a village on a ridge that drains south to the Conestoga River.
evidence.quote: Pennsylvania Route 23 is the community's Main Street

evidence.claim: The first settlers of the Lancaster Amish settlement settled nearby.
evidence.quote: The first settlers of the oldest Amish settlement still in existence, the Lancaster Amish settlement, settled near Churchtown.

evidence.claim: The village also includes Bangor Episcopal Church and the Edward Davies House, both on the National Register of Historic Places.
evidence.quote: The Bangor Episcopal Church, Caernarvon Presbyterian Church and Edward Davies House are listed on the National Register of Historic Places.

evidence.claim: Built about 1805, the stone Davies house combined a shop in its eastern section with living quarters to the west and an old kitchen at the rear.
evidence.quote: It was built about 1805

evidence.claim: The house’s T-shaped plan joins those three sections in a two-and-a-half-story Federal-style stone dwelling.
evidence.quote: It has three sections: the two bay eastern section that was originally Davies shop; the three bay western section that was originally his dwelling; and the rear "Old Kitchen" section.

evidence.claim: a village on a ridge that drains south to the Conestoga River.
evidence.quote: The community sits on a ridge draining south to the Conestoga River

evidence.claim: the stone Davies house
evidence.quote: T-shaped stone dwelling

evidence.claim: Bangor’s steeple came later than its brownstone walls.
evidence.quote: It has a steep, slate covered gable roof and steeple added about 1880.

evidence.claim: Built in 1830, the Churchtown church is a rectangular Gothic Revival building, with a steep slate roof and art-glass windows set in Gothic arches.
evidence.quote: The church was built in 1830, and is a 1 1/2-story, brownstone rectangular building in the Gothic Revival style.

evidence.claim: The steeple was added about 1880.
evidence.quote: steeple added about 1880.

evidence.claim: A frame school building from 1844 belongs to the same complex, but uses the Greek Revival style.
evidence.quote: The complex includes the frame school building.  It is a one-story, three bay building built in 1844 in the Greek Revival style.

evidence.claim: The churchyard contains graves dating from the Revolutionary War onward.
evidence.quote: a contributing cemetery with approximately 325 graves dated from the Revolutionary War to the present.

evidence.claim: The complex entered the National Register of Historic Places in 1978.
evidence.quote: It was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1978.

evidence.claim: art-glass windows set in Gothic arches.
evidence.quote: It features Gothic arch art glass windows.

evidence.claim: A ridge road above farm valleys, through Goodville and Churchtown.
evidence.quote: Following the ridge, overlooking sweeping views of the Conestoga River and valleys

evidence.claim: through Goodville and Churchtown.
evidence.quote: along with the communities of Goodville and Churchtown.

evidence.claim: PennDOT’s byway record also notes that local ordinances prohibit off-premise signs along the designated road.
evidence.quote: CONESTOGA RIDGE BYWAY Effective: 2013 District: 8-0 County: Lancaster State Route: 23 Conestoga Ridge includes PA Route 23 Main Street at Route 10 South and ends on Route 23 at Route 322 in Lancaster County, between Caernarvon and East Earl Townships. The prohibition of off-premise signs is enforced by local ordinances.

evidence.claim: At Blue Ball, the crossroads has an earlier history: John Wallace built his inn where the Native American French Creek Path met the Paxtang trail.
evidence.quote: John Wallace built a small building in Earl Town at the intersection of two trails created by native Americans, French Creek Path (Route 23) and Paxtang (Route 322).

evidence.claim: The inn stood on the southeastern corner of that intersection.
evidence.quote: stood on the southeastern corner of the PA 23-US 322 crossroads.

evidence.claim: The school is a single-story building with three bays, a smaller companion to the church.
evidence.quote: It is a one-story, three bay building

evidence.claim: Look for Gothic arches in the art-glass windows and the steep slate roof.
evidence.quote: It has a steep, slate covered gable roof and steeple added about 1880.  It features Gothic arch art glass windows.

evidence.claim: The house’s T-shaped plan joins those three sections in a two-and-a-half-story Federal-style stone dwelling.
evidence.quote: a 2+1⁄2-story, T-shaped stone dwelling with a gable roof in the Federal style.
